Monday’s remaining fixtures stay upcoming at the cutoff.

cards.title: U.S. strike near Hormuz ends a month-long lull
cards.summary: U.S. forces hit two Iranian launchers on Larak Island after officials said IRGC crews were preparing sea mines; Iran then reported missile retaliation against U.S. sites in Jordan.
detail: The Associated Press reported that U.S. forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island on Aug. 30 after the U.S. Central Command said Revolutionary Guard forces were preparing rockets carrying sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz. AP said Iran later reported missile attacks on U.S. sites in Jordan, while Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.

The immediate significance is maritime and regional: the strike came days after CENTCOM said international shipping lanes had been cleared of mines, while commercial traffic through the strait remained constrained. A military claim that a threat was removed does not establish that shipping has returned to normal.

The evidence is clear about the U.S. announcement and the reported Iranian response, but casualty and damage claims remain contested. The next uncertainty is whether the exchange stays limited or becomes a wider interruption to Gulf security and energy flows.
cards.why: The new exchange changes the security picture around the world’s key energy chokepoint.
verifiedFacts: AP reported U.S. strikes on two launchers on Larak Island.
The U.S. military said the launchers were associated with a mine threat in Hormuz.
Iranian media reported retaliation and Jordan reported intercepting eight missiles.
attributedClaims: CENTCOM described the action as limited and precise; Iranian state media described the response as retaliation.
analysis: The exchange raises the risk that a mine-clearance and reopening effort will be reversed.
uncertainty: The full damage and casualty tolls, future shipping access, and the scope of any retaliation remain unsettled.
conflicts: U.S. and Iranian accounts characterize the exchange differently.

cards.title: Ohio’s motor-voter injunction moves into appeal
cards.summary: The preliminary injunction remains the operative change at BMV offices while Secretary of State Frank LaRose pursues an immediate appeal.
detail: A federal judge’s Aug. 25 preliminary injunction blocks Ohio from relying on House Bill 54’s documentary-proof requirement before offering voter registration to eligible driver-license applicants at BMV offices. The order does not require an affirmative offer to applicants who identify as noncitizens or otherwise provide information showing they are not citizens.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose announced an immediate appeal, so the practical rule is now tied to litigation rather than a settled change in election administration. The court’s reasoning focused on the federal National Voter Registration Act and the added proof requirement.

The next uncertainty is whether the appeal changes the injunction before the Oct. 5 registration deadline. The state’s description of the case and the court’s order should remain separate: the injunction is verified, while the appeal’s outcome is not.

analysis: The appeal keeps the registration process unsettled ahead of the midterms.
